claim: It is common to find considerable genetic variation in susceptibility to infection in natural populations.
source: It is common to find considerable genetic variation in susceptibility to infection in natural populations (Chapman and Hill, 2012; Bangham et al., 2008a; Hammond-Kosack and Jones, 1997; Lazzaro et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Genetic variation in susceptibility can determine the impact of disease on health and economic output.
source: This variation in susceptibility can determine the impact of disease on health and economic output (Cooke and Hill, 2001; King and Lively, 2012; Alonso-Blanco and Méndez-Vigo, 2014; Burgner et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Genetic variation in susceptibility determines the ability of populations to evolve resistance to infection.
source: In nature and breeding programs, it determines the ability of populations to evolve resistance to infection.
evidence: Based on established understanding of evolutionary biology

claim: Insect populations typically contain considerable genetic variation in susceptibility to infection.
source: Insect populations, like those of other organisms, typically contain considerable genetic variation in susceptibility to infection (Bangham et al., 2008a; Lazzaro et al., 2004; Tinsley et al., 2006; Obbard and Dudas, 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Insect populations provide a convenient laboratory model to investigate questions about how genetic variation is maintained.
source: Insect populations, like those of other organisms, typically contain considerable genetic variation in susceptibility to infection (Bangham et al., 2008a; Lazzaro et al., 2004; Tinsley et al., 2006; Obbard and Dudas, 2014), and provide a convenient laboratory model in which to investigate basic questions about how this variation is maintained (Magwire et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Resistant mosquito genotypes are less likely to transmit pathogens.
source: Within vector species like mosquitoes, resistant genotypes are less likely to transmit pathogens, and this has the potential to reduce disease in vertebrate populations (Beerntsen et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: High levels of genetic variation may allow pollinator populations to recover when pathogens contribute to their decline.
source: Where pathogens are contributing the decline of beneficial species like pollinators, high levels of genetic variation may allow populations to recover (Maori et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and logical inference

claim: Natural selection is expected to favour resistant host genotypes.
source: As pathogens are harmful, natural selection is expected to favour resistant host genotypes.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary theory

claim: Directional selection on standing genetic variation will drive alleles to fixation, removing variants from the population.
source: Directional selection on standing genetic variation will drive alleles to fixation, removing variants from the population (Falconer, 1960; Falconer and Mackay, 1996; Blows and Hoffmann, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: At equilibrium, directional selection is expected to have no effect on levels of standing genetic variation relative to mutation-drift balance.
source: However, as directional selection also increases the frequency of new mutations that change the trait in the direction of selection, at equilibrium it is expected to have no effect on levels of standing genetic variation (relative to mutation-drift balance; Hill, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Coevolution with pathogens can result in the maintenance of both resistant and susceptible alleles by negative frequency dependent selection.
source: Coevolution with pathogens can result in the maintenance of both resistant and susceptible alleles by negative frequency dependent selection (Woolhouse et al., 2002; Haldane, 1949).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: When infection prevalence exhibits geographical or temporal variation, selection can maintain genetic variation, especially if pleiotropic costs to resistance provide an advantage to susceptible individuals when infection is rare.
source: Similarly, when infection prevalence exhibits geographical or temporal variation, selection can maintain genetic variation, especially if pleiotropic costs to resistance provide an advantage to susceptible individuals when infection is rare (Nuismer et al., 2003; Thompson, 1999; Koskella, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Directional selection can transiently increase genetic variation during the spread of rare alleles through the population.
source: If selection favours rare alleles – such as new mutations – directional selection can transiently increase genetic variation during their spread through the population (Barton and Turelli, 1987; Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There was more genetic variation in D. melanogaster susceptibility to two viruses isolated from D. melanogaster than to two viruses from other insect species.
source: As part of a whole genome association study, we have previously estimated levels of genetic variation in the susceptibility of D. melanogaster to four different viruses (Magwire et al., 2012). We found that there was more genetic variation in susceptibility to the two viruses that were isolated from D. melanogaster than the two viruses from other insect species.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: In each naturally coevolved D. melanogaster-virus association, a single major-effect polymorphism affecting resistance was detected.
source: Furthermore, in each of these naturally coevolved host-pathogen associations we detected a single major-effect polymorphism affecting resistance.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: Sigma viruses are a clade of insect RNA viruses with negative-sense genomes in the family Rhabdoviridae.
source: Sigma viruses are a clade of insect RNA viruses with negative-sense genomes in the family Rhabdoviridae (Longdon et al., 2017; Longdon et al., 2015a; Longdon et al., 2010; Longdon et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sigma viruses are vertically transmitted through eggs and sperm.
source: They are vertically transmitted through eggs and sperm, and each sigma virus infects a single host species, simplifying studies of coevolution (Longdon et al., 2017; Longdon et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Each sigma virus infects a single host species.
source: They are vertically transmitted through eggs and sperm, and each sigma virus infects a single host species, simplifying studies of coevolution (Longdon et al., 2017; Longdon et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In D. melanogaster, sigma virus infection reduces host fitness by approximately 25%.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, despite the virus causing little adult mortality, infection reduces host fitness by approximately 25% (Wilfert and Jiggins, 2013; Yampolsky et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sigma virus prevalence in wild D. melanogaster populations is typically around 10%.
source: As prevalence in wild populations is typically around 10% (Wilfert and Jiggins, 2013), there is the necessary selective pressure for resistance to evolve (Magwire et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Three major-effect resistance alleles have been identified in D. melanogaster against sigma virus.
source: In D. melanogaster, three major-effect resistance alleles have been identified (Bangham et al., 2008a; Magwire et al., 2012; Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2016; Bangham et al., 2008b; Wayne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There has been a recent sweep of D. melanogaster sigma virus genotypes that are able to overcome one of the host resistance genes.
source: There has been a recent sweep of D. melanogaster sigma virus (DMelSV) genotypes that are able to overcome one of these host resistance genes (Fleuriet, 1988; Wilfert and Jiggins, 2010a; Wilfert and Jiggins, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The four Drosophila species used in the study shared a common ancestor approximately 40 million years ago.
source: In this study we have used four species of Drosophila (D. affinis, D. immigrans, D. melanogaster and D. obscura) that shared a common ancestor approximately 40 million years ago (Obbard et al., 2012; Tamura et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The four sigma viruses have amino acid identities of <55% in the most conserved gene.
source: and their natural sigma viruses (DAffSV, DImmSV, DMelSV and DObsSV, which have amino acid identities of <55% in the most conserved gene) (Longdon et al., 2015a; Longdon et al., 2010; Longdon et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The phylogenies of sigma viruses and their hosts are incongruent, suggesting host jumps during evolution.
source: Despite their vertical mode of transmission, the phylogenies of the viruses and their hosts are incongruent, suggesting they have jumped between host species during their evolution (Longdon et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: In total, 52,592 flies were infected and viral load was measured in 4295 biological replicates across 1436 full-sib families.
source: In total we infected 52,592 flies and measured the viral load in 4295 biological replicates (a vial containing a mean of 12 flies) across 1436 full-sib families (details of sample sizes in Additional Methods).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Within populations of all four species, there was significantly greater genetic variance in susceptibility to the sigma virus that naturally infects that species compared to viruses from other species.
source: Within populations of all four species, we found significantly greater genetic variance in susceptibility to the sigma virus that naturally infects that species compared to viruses from other species (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in figures and supplementary files

claim: When families of D. obscura in the 2nd and 98th percentile were compared, there was a 1294 fold difference between the viral loads of the coevolved virus.
source: For example, when families of D. obscura in the 2nd and 98th percentile were compared, there was a 1294 fold difference between the viral loads of the coevolved virus in the families (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: For non-coevolved viruses in D. obscura, there was a 27 fold difference in DMelSV loads and a 19 fold difference in DAffSV loads between families in the 2nd and 98th percentile.
source: In contrast, for the non-coevolved viruses there was a 27 fold difference in DMelSV loads and a 19 fold difference in DAffSV loads (see Figure 2A for statistics).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Across the four species, there was no consistent difference between the mean viral load in coevolved versus non-coevolved associations.
source: The data in Figure 2 is zero-centred to allow comparison of the variances, but across the four species, there was no consistent difference between the mean viral load in coevolved versus non-coevolved associations (i.e. the coevolved virus does not always replicate to higher levels suggesting this is not an artefact of simply replicating poorly in a host – see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In D. melanogaster, the genetic correlation in viral loads between DMelSV and DAffSV was 0.40 (95% CIs: 0.20, 0.61).
source: In D. melanogaster these were 0.40 for DMelSV-DAffSV, (95% CIs: 0.20, 0.61) and 0.25 for DMelSV-DObsSV (95% CIs: −0.01,0.47).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In D. melanogaster, the genetic correlation in viral loads between DMelSV and DObsSV was 0.25 (95% CIs: −0.01,0.47).
source: In D. melanogaster these were 0.40 for DMelSV-DAffSV, (95% CIs: 0.20, 0.61) and 0.25 for DMelSV-DObsSV (95% CIs: −0.01,0.47).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In D. melanogaster, a substantial proportion of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV is explained by major-effect variants in the genes CHKov1 and p62.
source: In D. melanogaster a substantial proportion of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV is explained by major-effect variants in the genes CHKov1 and p62 (also known as Ref(2)P) (Magwire et al., 2012; Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011; Wayne et al., 1996; Contamine et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The resistant allele in CHKov1 and p62 has arisen recently by mutation and been driven up in frequency by natural selection, presumably due to the presence of DMelSV in natural populations.
source: The resistant allele in each of these genes has arisen recently by mutation and been driven up in frequency by natural selection, presumably due to the presence of DMelSV in natural populations (Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The load of DMelSV was more than halved in homozygous CHKov1 resistant flies compared to susceptible flies (reduction in log2 viral load = 1.2, 95% CI = 0.6, 1.8).
source: Assuming the effects of the resistant alleles are additive, we estimated that the load of the coevolved virus DMelSV was more than halved in homozygous CHKov1 resistant flies compared to susceptible flies (reduction in log2 viral load = 1.2, 95% CI = 0.6, 1.8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: CHKov1 had no significant effect on loads of the non-coevolved viruses DAffSV and DObsSV.
source: In contrast we found no significant effect of this gene on loads of the non-coevolved viruses (DAffSV = −0.2, 95% CI = 0.2,–0.8; DObsSV = −0.4, 95% CI = −0.04, 1.0).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The resistant allele of p62 was present at a low frequency (1.5%) in the D. melanogaster population.
source: The resistant allele of p62 was present at such a low frequency (1.5%) in the population that we lacked statistical power to investigate its effects.
evidence: Experimental data from genotyping

claim: The effect of CHKov1 and p62 genotypes was greater on DMelSV load than on DAffSV or DObsSV loads in 32 inbred D. melanogaster lines.
source: To confirm these results we infected 1869 flies from 32 inbred D. melanogaster lines (Mackay et al., 2012) that had known CHKov1 or p62 genotypes. The effect of these genes was greater on the naturally occurring virus than the viruses from other species (Figure 3; effect of genotype on DMelSV load: F2,28 = 13.2, p=0.00001; DAffSV: F2,29 = 4.9, p=0.01; DObsSV: F2,29 = 5.7, p=0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: The DSPR mapping population samples genetic variation in a small number of genotypes from around the world.
source: This population samples genetic variation in a small number of genotypes from around the world (the experiments above sampled many genotypes from a single location).
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: 377 recombinant inbred lines from the DSPR populations were used, which have up to 15 alleles of each gene.
source: We used 377 RILs from these populations, which have up to 15 alleles of each gene (one founder line is shared between the two populations).
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: 15,916 flies across 1362 biological replicates were infected with DMelSV, DAffSV or DObsSV in the DSPR mapping experiment.
source: We infected 15,916 flies across 1362 biological replicates (a vial containing a mean of 12 flies) with DMelSV, DAffSV or DObsSV and measured viral load as above (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: In the DSPR mapping population, there was considerably more genetic variation in susceptibility to the coevolved virus DMelSV than the non-coevolved viruses.
source: We first estimated the genetic variance in viral load within our mapping population. The results recapitulated what we had found above in a natural population of flies — there was considerably more genetic variation in susceptibility to the coevolved virus than the non-coevolved viruses (Figure 4A, filled circles).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4A

claim: Seven QTL affecting DMelSV load were identified in the DSPR mapping population.
source: In the coevolved association (DMelSV) we identified seven QTL associated with resistance, compared to one that affects DObsSV and none affecting DAffSV (Supplementary file 5; this excludes one DMelSV QTL on the X chromosome that did not remain significant after accounting for the other QTL).
evidence: QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5

claim: One QTL affecting DObsSV load was identified in the DSPR mapping population.
source: In the coevolved association (DMelSV) we identified seven QTL associated with resistance, compared to one that affects DObsSV and none affecting DAffSV (Supplementary file 5; this excludes one DMelSV QTL on the X chromosome that did not remain significant after accounting for the other QTL).
evidence: QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5

claim: No QTL affecting DAffSV load were identified in the DSPR mapping population.
source: In the coevolved association (DMelSV) we identified seven QTL associated with resistance, compared to one that affects DObsSV and none affecting DAffSV (Supplementary file 5; this excludes one DMelSV QTL on the X chromosome that did not remain significant after accounting for the other QTL).
evidence: QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5

claim: The QTL affecting DObsSV also has a significant effect on DMelSV.
source: The QTL affecting DObsSV also has a significant effect on DMelSV.
evidence: QTL mapping analysis

claim: One of the QTL identified in the DSPR mapping corresponds to p62 (2L 53 cM).
source: One of the QTL corresponded to p62 (2L 53 cM).
evidence: QTL mapping analysis

claim: The susceptible allele of CHKov1 was not present in the DSPR fly lines assayed.
source: The susceptible allele of CHKov1 was not present in the fly lines assayed.
evidence: Genotyping data

claim: Six of the seven QTL resulted in greater reductions in the load of the coevolved virus DMelSV than the viruses isolated from other species.
source: Six of the seven QTL resulted in greater reductions in the load of the coevolved virus (DMelSV) than the viruses isolated from other species (Figure 4C).
evidence: QTL effect analysis presented in Figure 4C

claim: Resistant alleles at the identified QTL cause an approximate 3–7 fold reduction in viral load.
source: Individually, resistant alleles cause an approximate 3–7 fold reduction in viral load (Figure 4C)
evidence: QTL effect analysis presented in Figure 4C

claim: The identified QTL together explain 59% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV.
source: and together they explain 59% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV, 77% for DObsSV and 3% for DAffSV (Figure 4A, filled versus open circles).
evidence: Statistical analysis of QTL effects presented in Figure 4A

claim: The identified QTL together explain 77% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DObsSV.
source: and together they explain 59% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV, 77% for DObsSV and 3% for DAffSV (Figure 4A, filled versus open circles).
evidence: Statistical analysis of QTL effects presented in Figure 4A

claim: The identified QTL together explain 3% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DAffSV.
source: and together they explain 59% of the genetic variance in susceptibility to DMelSV, 77% for DObsSV and 3% for DAffSV (Figure 4A, filled versus open circles).
evidence: Statistical analysis of QTL effects presented in Figure 4A

claim: Even after accounting for the identified QTL, there remains a significantly higher genetic variance in the viral load of the coevolved virus.
source: However, even after accounting for these genes there remains a significantly higher genetic variance in the viral load of the coevolved virus (Figure 4A, open circles, non-overlapping 95% CI).
evidence: Statistical analysis presented in Figure 4A

claim: Selection by pathogens has acted to increase the amount of genetic variation in susceptibility.
source: We have found greater genetic variation in susceptibility to viruses that naturally infect Drosophila compared to viruses that do not, suggesting that selection by these pathogens has acted to increase the amount of genetic variation in susceptibility.
evidence: Inference from experimental results showing greater genetic variation in coevolved associations

claim: The increased genetic variation in coevolved associations was largely caused by a modest number of major-effect genes that explain over half of the genetic variance in resistance.
source: This effect was largely caused by a modest number of major-effect genes that explain over half of the genetic variance in resistance.
evidence: Inference from QTL mapping results

claim: In both p62 and CHKov1, the resistant alleles have arisen relatively recently by mutation and natural selection has pushed them rapidly up in frequency.
source: In both these genes the resistant alleles have arisen relatively recently by mutation and natural selection has pushed them rapidly up in frequency, leaving a characteristic signature of elevated linkage disequilibrium and low genetic diversity around the variant causing resistance (Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011; Wayne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There is no indication of negative frequency dependent selection on p62 and CHKov1, and these polymorphisms appear to have arisen from partial selective sweeps.
source: There is no indication of negative frequency dependent selection, and these polymorphisms appear to have arisen from partial selective sweeps (Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The most parsimonious explanation of the observations is that there has been directional selection favouring resistance alleles.
source: The most parsimonious explanation of these observations is that there has been directional selection favouring resistance alleles (although this type of data cannot rule out negative frequency dependent selection as is predicted by models of coevolution).
evidence: Inference from patterns of DNA sequence variation

claim: The genetic variance will transiently increase if the variants under selection are initially at low frequency.
source: However, the genetic variance will transiently increase if the variants under selection are initially at low frequency (Barton and Turelli, 1987), as was the case for both p62 and CHKov1 (Bangham et al., 2007; Magwire et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to theory and empirical data

claim: In France and Germany in the 1980s, DMelSV evolved to largely overcome the effects of the resistant allele of p62.
source: For example, in France and Germany in the 1980s, DMelSV evolved to largely overcome the effects of the resistant allele of p62 (Fleuriet and Periquet, 1993; Fleuriet and Sperlich, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DImmSV has swept through European populations of D. immigrans in the last ~16 years.
source: Similarly, DImmSV has swept through European populations of D. immigrans in the last ~16 years and DObsSV through UK populations of D. obscura in the last ~11 years (Longdon et al., 2017; Longdon et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DObsSV has swept through UK populations of D. obscura in the last ~11 years.
source: Similarly, DImmSV has swept through European populations of D. immigrans in the last ~16 years and DObsSV through UK populations of D. obscura in the last ~11 years (Longdon et al., 2017; Longdon et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: If selection by pathogens continually changes and resistance evolves from new mutations, this may cause a sustained increase in genetic variance in susceptibility to infection.
source: If selection by pathogens continually changes and resistance evolves from new mutations, then this may cause a sustained increase in genetic variance in susceptibility to infection.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on evolutionary theory

claim: Theory suggests that a critical factor determining levels of genetic variation is whether resistance is costly to evolve.
source: Theory suggests that a critical factor determining levels of genetic variation is whether resistance is costly to evolve, as this can result in the maintenance of variation by negative frequency dependent selection (Antonovics and Thrall, 1994; Boots et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical research

claim: In humans, there is less genetic variation in susceptibility to pathogens that are effectively controlled by the adaptive immune response, possibly because these resistance mechanisms may be less costly.
source: In humans this has been proposed as an explanation of why there is less genetic variation in susceptibility to pathogens that are effectively controlled by the adaptive immune response, as these resistance mechanisms may be less costly (Baker and Antonovics, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: It seems unlikely that virus resistance in Drosophila is costly, as experiments have failed to detect costs of DCV resistance.
source: However, it seems unlikely that virus resistance in Drosophila is costly, as experiments have failed to detect costs of DCV resistance (Faria et al., 2015) despite costs of parasitoid and bacterial resistance being repeatedly detected (McGonigle et al., 2017; McKean et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sigma viruses are extreme host specialists.
source: Sigma viruses are also extreme host specialists, so evolutionary changes in resistance will tend to alter pathogen prevalence and so the strength of selection.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sigma viruses

claim: Epidemiological feedbacks are predicted to frequently increase genetic diversity.
source: These epidemiological feedbacks are predicted to frequently increase genetic diversity (Boots et al., 2014; Best et al., 2009; Boots and Haraguchi, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical research

claim: In D. melanogaster, there are large amounts of genetic variation in susceptibility to viruses that have a broader host range than sigma viruses.
source: However, in D. melanogaster we see large amounts of genetic variation in susceptibility to viruses that have a broader host range than sigma viruses (DCV and Kallithea virus that infect D. melanogaster and D. simulans in the wild) (Magwire et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2018; Christian, 1987; Webster et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In wild flax plants, sympatric (putatively coevolved) populations had fewer partial resistances than allopatric populations, suggesting more major gene effects.
source: In an analogous study of rust resistance in wild flax plants, sympatric (putatively coevolved) populations had fewer partial resistances than allopatric populations, suggesting more major gene effects, even though overall there was somewhat less genetic variation in susceptibility to sympatric fungal pathogens (Antonovics et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Quantitative traits are typically controlled by a very large number of genetic variants, each of which tends to have a very small effect.
source: Quantitative traits are typically controlled by a very large number of genetic variants, each of which tends to have a very small effect (Shi et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Susceptibility to sigma viruses has a simpler genetic basis, with seven polymorphisms explaining over half the genetic variance.
source: However, susceptibility to sigma viruses has a simpler genetic basis, with seven polymorphisms explaining over half the genetic variance.
evidence: Experimental results from QTL mapping

claim: Most quantitative traits are under stabilising selection, so major effect variants will tend to be deleterious and removed by selection.
source: One explanation for this observation is that most quantitative traits are under stabilising selection, so major effect variants will tend to be deleterious and removed by selection (Gibson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Fisher's geometric model predicts that major effect variants will be favoured by directional selection when populations are far from their optimal level of resistance.
source: In contrast, selection by pathogens likely changes through time and populations may be far from their optimal level of resistance. If this is the case, Fisher's geometric model predicts that major effect variants will be favoured by directional selection (Fisher, 1930).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical model

claim: The coevolution of hosts and parasites can favour discrete susceptible and resistant hosts.
source: Alternatively, the coevolution of hosts and parasites can favour discrete susceptible and resistant hosts (Boots et al., 2014), and at the genetic level this may result in major-effect variants (although this theory does not explicitly address the underlying genetics).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical research

claim: For virus resistance, a single loss of function mutation may prevent a virus binding to a host receptor or utilising other parts of the host cellular machinery, and so confer strong resistance.
source: For example a single (loss of function) mutation may prevent a virus binding to a host receptor or utilising other parts of the host cellular machinery, and so confer strong resistance.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on biological knowledge

claim: Hill (2012) advocated the view that susceptibility to infectious disease is qualitatively different from other traits and has a much simpler genetic basis.
source: In humans, Hill (2012) advocated the view that susceptibility to infectious disease is qualitatively different from other traits and has a much simpler genetic basis (Hill, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: In Drosophila, resistance to DCV and parasitoid wasps both have a simple genetic basis.
source: In Drosophila, resistance to DCV and parasitoid wasps both have a simple genetic basis (Magwire et al., 2012; Cao et al., 2017; Orr and Irving, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In plants, major-effect polymorphisms in R genes are commonplace.
source: In plants, major-effect polymorphisms in R genes are commonplace (Hammond-Kosack and Jones, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: In a plant-fungi system, genotype-by-genotype interactions explain a larger proportion of the total variance in sympatric (more coevolved) associations.
source: and in a plant-fungi system genotype-by-genotype interactions explain a larger proportion of the total variance in sympatric (more coevolved) associations (Antonovics et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Studies of bacterial resistance in Drosophila have typically used pathogens that are unlikely to have any history of coevolution, and have found a polygenic basis to resistance.
source: In contrast, studies of bacterial resistance in Drosophila have typically used pathogens that are unlikely to have any history of coevolution, and have found a polygenic basis to resistance (Bou Sleiman et al., 2015; Hotson and Schneider, 2015; Howick and Lazzaro, 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The polymorphism with the largest effect in bacterial resistance studies was found against the only natural D. melanogaster pathogen tested (a polymorphism in Diptericin detected using Providencia rettgeri infection).
source: In these studies the polymorphism with the largest effect was found against the only natural D. melanogaster pathogen tested (a polymorphism in Diptericin detected using Providencia rettgeri infection), anecdotally supporting the patterns seen here (Howick and Lazzaro, 2017; Unckless et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A major source of emerging infectious disease is pathogens jumping into novel hosts where they have no co-evolutionary history.
source: A major source of emerging infectious disease is pathogens jumping into novel hosts where they have no co-evolutionary history (Longdon et al., 2014; Parrish et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: When a pathogen infects a novel host species, there may be far less genetic variation in susceptibility among individuals than is normally the case.
source: Our results suggest that when a pathogen infects a novel host species, there may be far less genetic variation in susceptibility among individuals than is normally the case.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: Low genetic variation in novel host-pathogen associations may create a 'monoculture effect', which could leave populations vulnerable to epidemics.
source: This may create a 'monoculture effect' (King and Lively, 2012; Lively, 2010; Ostfeld and Keesing, 2012), which could leave populations vulnerable to epidemics of pathogens that have previously circulated in other host species.
evidence: Inference from experimental results combined with cited theory

claim: Low levels of pre-standing genetic variation may slow down the rate at which a new host can evolve resistance to a new pathogen.
source: Longer term, low levels of pre-standing genetic variation may slow down the rate at which the new host can evolve resistance to a new pathogen.
evidence: Inference from experimental results and evolutionary theory

claim: Selection by pathogens has increased the amount of genetic variation in host susceptibility.
source: In conclusion, we have demonstrated that selection by pathogens has increased the amount of genetic variation in host susceptibility.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental results

claim: Resistance to sigma viruses is largely controlled by major effect resistance loci.
source: We find resistance has a simple underlying genetic architecture and is largely controlled by major effect resistance loci.
evidence: Conclusion based on QTL mapping results

claim: Studies on DMelSV have shown that loci that reduce loads when the virus is injected also reduce infection rates in both the lab and field.
source: Studies on DMelSV have shown that loci that reduce loads when the virus is injected also reduce infection rates in both the lab and field (Bangham et al., 2008a; Longdon et al., 2012; Bregliano, 1970; Brun and Plus, 1980; Ohanessian-Guillemain, 1963; Wilfert and Jiggins, 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Loci that reduce viral loads when the virus is injected are expected to increase host fitness.
source: As infection is costly, this is expected to increase host fitness.
